messages.subject: allometry-free modularity tests -- logic & method?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question on using allometry “free” shapes to estimate modularity at different developmental stages - how it should be done or if it even makes sense.

I’m focusing on 2 species for which I’ve already shown ontogenetic allometries differ. I am curious if different regions of the skull show different patterns of modularity between species and stages, e.g. neonate, juvenile, adult.

Using the covariance ratio (CR) I see that the strength of modularity changes markedly between the juvenile and adult stages, and I am now wondering if it makes sense to also test this using regression residuals, because 1) I’m specifically interested in how ontogeny (i.e., size) affects trait correlations within the skull given developmental benchmarks like suckling and weaning, and 2) because the species have significantly different allometric slopes.

Mike has previously written here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/geomorph-r-package/1jXm_6dNE3A> that “you cannot remove heterogenous allometric variation but must address the separate allometric patterns when making comparisons among groups”. I considered using the residuals from the species-specific anova (procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logsize * Species, data = gdf, print.progress = FALSE) to estimate size-free shapes for use with modularity.test, which I can do but I’m not sure the results would be correct or even meaningful. I’m also asking because I have seen it done in other papers and am unclear of the logic or interpretation. The only reason I can think of is to compare with the “full” shape modularity results to show that size/ontogeny is a driving factor, although with an ontogenetic data set where I already know size is significant, I don’t see why this would be important.

Thanks for any advice on how or if I should move forward with this approach.

Christy

Hi Christy

In general, in terms of dealing with a situation like what Mike wrote (“you cannot remove heterogenous allometric variation but must address the separate allometric patterns when making comparisons among groups”), I would not simply use evidence of significance of the interaction between species:size (or ontogeny). One thing I often have found is that even when such an interaction term shows statistically significant differences, the angle (or correlation) between vectors (i.e. the allometry vectors for each species) suggest they are very similar. i.e. the angle is near zero (correlation near 1).  This is often observed for us with static allometry vectors in Drosophila (where we have relatively large sample sizes in our experiments). So you may wish to do some additional evaluation (including the vector correlations, R^2 etc) and visual checks (maybe with some predicted values at extreme values) to determine whether the differences are likely to be meaningful (given your understanding of the biology of these organisms etc). Also, this depends on your sample sizes. If you have relatively modest sample sizes, and evidence for a species:size effect, that starts to suggest (but still check) that the allometric vectors may be different enough to warrant some concern.  Often in such cases I test whether the assumption of common allometry makes a real difference or not and report BOTH (never do both analyses and only report one).  Chris Klingenberg talks a little bit about this issue in his allometry opus from a couple of years ago in Development, Genes and Evolution.

Since you are doing ontogenic allometry the effects are likely pretty big (as compared to static allometry within species).

Hope this helps a bit in thinking about the problem.

Ian

messages.body_plain:
One of the main reasons for removing the effects of allometry in studies comparing integration/modularity across ontogeny is that age-classes are often heterogeneous in age; the mean shape changes over the span of the age-class so you risk confounding that change in the mean with the variation around the mean. Even if your age-classes are not that heterogenous, you might still risk confounding ontogenetic change with variation if individuals differ in rates of growth and/or development, variation that is transient although perhaps interesting. The other main reason, which is not specific to ontogenetic studies, is that size is a "global" factor, and the integration due to that might obscure more local (modular) processes. Even if you don't get statistically significant differences, erring on the side of caution in these studies would motivate using species (and perhaps also stage-specific) allometries if the ontogenetic trajectories curve.  You might lack the power to determine that the difference is significant, but you don't want to risk incorporating the deviations from common-slope model into the analysis of modularity

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Miriam and Ian for your responses.

In my case the 2 species in question are statistically different in ontogenetic allometries, yet still very similar in slope vector length (d=0.026, p=0.003) and slope vector angle (correlation [r] =0.911, angle=24.402 degrees, p=0.001). Even so, if I were to adjust for size to run modularity tests, can I use the residuals from the species-specific anova (procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logsize * Species)), or I remove size for the common allometry using procD.lm(Pcoords ~ logsize) given how similar they actually are? Doing either of these gives very different results, at least looking at their PCAs.

Thanks again for your feedback. It's helpful to think of these questions in terms of real biology, as you both suggested.

In this case, I'd say to use the species'-specific allometries because you aren't making any strong claims about the difference, and therefore don't need to worry about exaggerating a difference that is slight. The point is to avoid introducing what you might perceive as variation (within age) when that variation is the deviation from a misfitting model.

messages.body_plain:
Christy

 How many landmarks do you have? Depending on this (also 2D or 3D)  a vector correlation of 0.91 may not be as similar as you suspect. I usually do a permutation test to generate a distribution of correlations under which can help get a sense of this given the number of landmarks (and covariance pattern among them).

However at a default (based on your results of a vector correlation of 0.91) I would be skeptical about whether an assumption of a common allometric relationship is warranted. Usually the situation I was mentioning in my previous response is when you get a significant interaction, but the correlation is still around 0.99.

Ian

> Thanks Miriam and Ian for your responses.

> On Saturday, August 3, 2019 at 2:16:57 AM UTC+10, Miriam Zelditch wrote:

> > One of the main reasons for removing the effects of allometry in studies comparing integration/modularity across ontogeny is that age-classes are often heterogeneous in age; the mean shape changes over the span of the age-class so you risk confounding that change in the mean with the variation around the mean. Even if your age-classes are not that heterogenous, you might still risk confounding ontogenetic change with variation if individuals differ in rates of growth and/or development, variation that is transient although perhaps interesting. The other main reason, which is not specific to ontogenetic studies, is that size is a "global" factor, and the integration due to that might obscure more local (modular) processes. Even if you don't get statistically significant differences, erring on the side of caution in these studies would motivate using species (and perhaps also stage-specific) allometries if the ontogenetic trajectories curve.  You might lack the power to determine that the difference is significant, but you don't want to risk incorporating the deviations from common-slope model into the analysis of modularity
> >

messages.subject: Potential omission of digitsurface from surface semilandmark analysis?
messages.subject_clean: Potential omission of digitsurface from surface semilandmark analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Hello geomorph community,

My reason for posting is that I've encountered an issue with digitizing surface semilandmarks with the function digitsurface.

I’m using 200 surface semilandmarks to look at juvenile clavicular shape change from 1-18yrs of age.  I’ve been using the following functions: digit.fixed to select 5 fixed landmarks across the clavicle, buildtemplate to create my semilandmark matrix and digitsurface.

When I run digitsurface my template semilandmarks that should be populating across the entirety of the clavicle (as they are in buildtemplate), are instead being digitized in clusters with some surfaces of the bone left bare.

I believe the cause of this issue is the result of my relatively low number of fixed landmarks and this might be causing an issue with the template matching? However, due to the nature of the juvenile clavicle it is difficult to find additional homolougus landmark sites beyond the 5 identified.

if I were to run buildtemplate for each of my specimens, would it possible to use the fixed and semilandmark matrix created by buildtemplate for each specimen in my analysis and avoid using digitsurface? Additionally, would the omission of digitsurface have negative ramifications for my analysis?

Thanks,
Sean

messages.body_plain:
Sean,

Unfortunately, running build template on each will not guarantee correspondence of semilandmarks across the specimens, so that is not an option I would advocate.

What you describe can happen with digit.surface; particularly when attempting to digitize all sides of a structure (e.g., a bone), and using only a few landmarks as reference. For context, that function was originally developed for relatively simple and flat 3D surfaces (scallop shells actually), and it is not optimized for all manner of 3D surfaces. In fact, it is quite hard to develop a general digitizing tool that is not ‘tweaked’ in some way for each particular application: see the recent paper by Anjali Goswami’s group on developing a digitizing pipeline for 3D objects.

One solution that has worked for some users, but still using geomorph, is to digitize some other points originally as ‘fixed’ that surround the structure to get digit.surface to behave a bit better. Then, at the gpagen step, treat these as sliding semilandmarks as they should be.

Good luck!

Dean

Hello geomorph community,

My reason for posting is that I've encountered an issue with digitizing surface semilandmarks with the function digitsurface.

I’m using 200 surface semilandmarks to look at juvenile clavicular shape change from 1-18yrs of age.  I’ve been using the following functions: digit.fixed to select 5 fixed landmarks across the clavicle, buildtemplate to create my semilandmark matrix and digitsurface.

When I run digitsurface my template semilandmarks that should be populating across the entirety of the clavicle (as they are in buildtemplate), are instead being digitized in clusters with some surfaces of the bone left bare.

I believe the cause of this issue is the result of my relatively low number of fixed landmarks and this might be causing an issue with the template matching? However, due to the nature of the juvenile clavicle it is difficult to find additional homolougus landmark sites beyond the 5 identified.

if I were to run buildtemplate for each of my specimens, would it possible to use the fixed and semilandmark matrix created by buildtemplate for each specimen in my analysis and avoid using digitsurface? Additionally, would the omission of digitsurface have negative ramifications for my analysis?

Thanks,

Sean

messages.body_plain:
This is done post-hoc prior to running gpagen.

Recall first that build.template not only digitizes points, but outputs a ‘surfslide.csv’ file. This file contains a list of all points that are to be considered sliding surface landmarks. One reads this into R as a vector, and when using gpagen, one provides this vector to the function in the ‘surface = XX’ location. If using some additional placeholder landmarks, what one does is simply appends their landmark positions to this list of sliding surface landmarks prior to running gpagen.

For example, say you digitize 5 fixed points, and an additional 10 for ‘helping’ the surface function.  You then generate 100 sliders. That results in 115 total points, and a list of surface sliders that goes 16 – 115.  Simply append that list to go from 6 – 115 and run through gpagen.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] testing trait ~ shape*sex
messages.body_plain:
Chris,

Here is an example of how to use shape variables to predict another continuous trait.  (I assume you wish to do that, otherwise you would just stick with measuring covariation, as you are doing.)  One caveat: although we often harp on using all shape variables in an analysis, that is to test hypotheses about shape.  When making predictions from shape, one might and probably should wish to restrict the aspects of shape used to predict the trait.  The reason for this is that you have to have a value for every shape variable to make a prediction.  Therefore, principal component analysis might be helpful.  Here is an example for how one can do this in RRPP, using the first three PCs.  I did this with some random data and the Pupfish shape data.  Note that you could use gm.prcomp and procD.lm in geomorph (in replace of ordinate and lm.rrpp, respectively) and get to the same place, but predict.lm.rrpp is an RRPP function.

data(Pupfish)
shape <- as.data.frame(ordinate(Pupfish$coords, rank.=3)$x) # first three PCs as shape variables
colnames(shape) <- c("p1", "p2", "p3")
trait <- rnorm(nrow(shape))
fit <- lm(trait ~ . , data = shape) # a trick to use all desired shape variables
fit <- lm.rrpp(fit)

pred.data <- data.frame(p1 = range(shape$p1), p2 = 0, p3 = 0) # extremes on PC 1
preds <- predict(fit, newdata = pred.data)
summary(preds)
plot(preds)

If you play around with this example, you might see how you could generate confidence intervals for your trait with respect to a certain aspect of shape.

You can also use shape * sex interactions, but in this case you had better only have few PCs or the multitude of permutations for which to make predictions can become intractable.  Another option is to perform shape analysis on all data but subset the shape variables into male and female sets before fitting the data and making predictions.  The confidence intervals are generated from bootstrap resampling, so this latter method would make sure to resample within sex.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] testing trait ~ shape*sex
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I’m not sure what your data used for prediction are exactly but if you followed my example strongly, then yes, you could say that shapes at the extremes of PC1 have sufficiently different bite force (because of non-overlapping CIs).  You could also make a sequenced vector, e.g.,

pc.steps <- seq(min(p1), max(p1), 0.1)

if you want to see if there is more of a gradual trend for bite force to change from one end of PC 1 to the other.  You call the shots, depending on the locations of values in a PC plot you think are appropriate (you could use PC scores for means of different groups, for example).

The ordinate function is relatively new, available on the Github version of RRPP.  You might be using the CRAN version or an older Github version.  The way you did it is fine though.

The approach you used to include sex works as long as you do not want to model any interactions.  The ~ . part is a trick for the lm function to include each variable in a data frame once.  It only works in rare situations.  You might rather do something like

trait ~ p1 * sex + p2 * sex

and then you would have to have a data frame for the newdata that has logical combinations of variables.  Note that including sex might be redundant if there is sexual dimorphism, as the observed pc scores would suggest different locations for males and females in a PC plot.  This is no trouble for the predict function!  It’s just that your inferences might be awkward if for example males all have positive PC 1 scores and females all have negative scores.  There would not naturally be a combination that includes females and positive pc scores, but if you feed the predict.lm.rrpp function such information, it will attempt to find a solution.

The more that I think about it, having an interaction between shape and sex might be kind of silly, unless there are differences in bite force between males and females not due to shape, in which case you might wish to account for sex (to have more precision in estimation).  If you are including sex because sexes differ in shape, it should be redundant information.

Hope that makes sense!
Mike

messages.subject: fixed.angle update
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph users,

I wish to alert you that I have made an update to the fixed.angle function, found currently on Github.  Starting with version 3.1, we started to allow multiple points to be used to define points for rotation (using the mean of points).  In updating that function, we inadvertently transposed the rotation matrix that was calculated in the fixed.angle function prior to version 3.1.  This seems like it would not be a big deal, as it should only change clockwise rotation to counter-clockwise rotation; i.e., if one before rotated some landmarks 10 degrees, they might now have to choose -10 degrees.  However, thanks to the example provided by Jenn Deitloff (thanks Jenn!), it appears to be a more dangerous problem to have the rotation matrix transposed.  Therefore, I updated the function to make sure the rotation matrix was the same as those calculated in the fixed.angle function before the 3.1 version of geomorph.

A couple of caveats:
1) This could mean for some users that they might have to update their code to change the sign of the angle they use.  If you update geomorph, use fixed.angle, and now your results are quite different, try changing the sign of your angle and see if the results return to normal.
2) If changing the sign of the angle does not return results to an expected state, please let us know.  With fixed.angle, it is difficult to pinpoint issues until we have data that reveal an issue.  (For example, Jenn’s example had specimens facing to the right and in testing the function, we used geomorph data, which tend to have specimens facing the left in 2D cases.  This helped to reveal that the matrix transposition was a problem.)

Have a great day!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] What is the difference between Procrustes ANOVA and MANOVA and how to do both in geomorph
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] What is the difference between Procrustes ANOVA and MANOVA and how to do both in geomorph
messages.body_plain:
YW,

The simple, imprecise answer is that Procrustes ANOVA and MANOVA are the same.  The M in MANOVA just indicates that the data are multivariate.  In the Quick Guide you are reading (not version 3.0.5, but older), they were treated as the same.

However, in more recent versions of geomorph, we have tried to not use these words interchangeably and more precisely use the word, ANOVA, to indicate the use of statistics calculated from the (Procrustes) distances of shapes from the overall mean or estimated values; i.e., these are univariate statistics (SS, MS, F values, etc.) based on distances, even if the data are multivariate.  This approach is nice because the number of variables has no influence on the statistics.

We now use a more precise definition of MANOVA to use multivariate test statistics (Wilks Lambda, Pillai trace, Hotelling-Lawley trace, Roy’s maximum root) rather than ANOVA statistics (SS, MS, Rsq, F).  Note that traditionally, parametric MANOVA would convert these statistics into approximate F values to infer “significance”.  The manova.update function (with more discussion of this on the help page) uses RRPP to generate distributions of multivariate test statistics.  Because multivariate test statistics are sensitive to the number of variables, there are also options for reducing data dimensionality.

The manova.update (RRPP function) help page and the vignette in the same package ("ANOVA vs MANOVA in RRPP") go into much more detail.

Note, the vignettes in RRPP and geomorph are always current with respect to the functions in those packages; the "quick guide" still exists but is no longer maintained with the geomorph package.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Hello Geomorph Users,

I am attempting to study craniofacial shape change following artificial selection in mice. There are three lines in the experiment, a random bred control (control line), and two replicates of the same selection regime (line 1 and 2). I have scans of individuals from the 1st (no selection), 10th and 20th generations for all three lines. I would like to control for the effect of allometry, as this is a common practice in the lab, and I am wondering if anyone can help me generate the proper linear model for this complex sample. First, I concatenated Line:Generation to generate 9 group factors (line1:gen1, line2:gen1 etc.) called group. Then I created linear_model using procD.lm() with coords ~ Csize*group to try and capture the unique allometry (I admit I do not know the differences between common and unique allometry). I plotted this model with plotAllometry() and found that the slopes do not differ using pairwise() with test.type = "VC" and angle.type = "deg". From there I attempted to extract the residuals to use in subsequent analyses. However, the residuals that I extract (linear_model$residuals) no longer resemble skulls whatsoever if I plot them with plotAllspecimens(). Is my model not valid for my sample, or am I just not extracting the correct residuals? I am very new to morphometrics and online sources are just confusing me. Any insights would be greatly appreciated if anyone can help!

Thanks
Colton U

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with estimate.missing function
messages.body_plain:
Dear Pablo,

I took a look at your data and the problem is obvious without even running the code.
All your specimens have landmark 15 missing.
The TPS method needs to have a reference specimen for which all landmarks are present. Withouth a complete specimen, neither the TPS nor the Regression method will work.
Please take a look at the "Details" section in the help section of the "estimate.missing" function. This text states:

The first approach (method="TPS") uses the thin-plate spline to interpolate landmarks on a reference specimen to estimate the locations of missing landmarks on a target specimen. Here, a reference specimen is obtained from the set of specimens for which all landmarks are present, Next, each incomplete specimen is aligned to the reference using the set of landmarks common to both. Finally, the thin-plate spline is used to estimate the locations of the missing landmarks in the target specimen.

So, without a complete specimen, no landmarks can be estimated!!

If the landmark is bilateral (i.e. is present on the other side) and your specimen has object symmetry, you could use reflected relabeling to estimate the missing landmarks. Note that this only works for bilateral homologues, so not if it is a unilateral landmark. Also note that this will make the esimated landmark symmetrical, while your specimens might have an inherent asymmetry (i.e. fluctuating or direction-based). Please consider your research question carefully, as symmetrizing a single landmark while maintaining assymetry in the rest of your sample could bias your results.

Best regards,
Abel
